generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, group work is common, from planning a coaching session together to a shared practical or field project, and tutors watch the process closely. They know that sport is collaborative, whether in a coaching team, a lab group or a rehabilitation clinic, and that someone who cannot listen, divide work fairly, or manage disagreement will struggle on any staff. The behaviours they assess, communication, listening, flexibility and accountability, are the ones sport itself runs on.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students are planning a group session plan, when a teammate proposes an unusual warm-up drill for the skill they are teaching.

Tom hears the suggestion, says 'sure, whatever works', and returns to his own part of the plan. The idea is neither built on nor questioned. Later Tom complains that the session felt disjointed. He heard the teammate but did not listen, because nothing was done with the contribution. This is participation without collaboration.

Amara hears the same suggestion and asks two questions about how the drill would progress and whether it suits the age group, then proposes folding part of it into the existing plan. The teammate feels heard, and the session improves. When a later task slips because a member is injured and cannot demonstrate, Amara takes on the coaching points rather than let the team stall. This is collaboration: listening turned into action, with accountability.

Both were in the meeting. Only Amara did the thing tutors are actually assessing.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, group work is assessed for its process because sport itself is collaborative. You can now explain why tutors value the process, tell real listening apart from merely hearing, and name the behaviour a situation is calling for. The next lesson looks at what happens when a team falls into conflict, and how to reflect on it.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that counts as listening rather than just hearing?

items.text: She asked how the drill would progress and folded part of it into the session plan.
She nodded along and said the idea was fine before moving on.
She wrote the idea down to mention in her reflective account.
She waited politely until the teammate had finished speaking.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara acted on the idea, which is what turns hearing into listening.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the idea, not how politely she received it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Listening meant asking about the drill and building part of it into the session plan. Nodding, noting it down, or simply waiting are all closer to hearing.
